headline: Medium risk: Chatwoot’s broad egress and customer-data handling can feed RisingWave workflows, creating leakage and cascading-error exposure; no direct shared-channel evidence is documented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Chatwoot can ingest external messages and integrations, while RisingWave has no documented input channel from Chatwoot. No shared filesystem or MCP bridge is shown, so a direct injection path is not evidenced. The only plausible bridge is manual or integration-mediated content transfer, which keeps this low rather than medium.
conditions: IF Chatwoot content is copied into RisingWave SQL, configs, or docs without sanitization
IF an operator wires Chatwoot outputs into a shared queue or file that RisingWave later parses as instructions
mitigations: Restrict Chatwoot-to-RisingWave transfers to structured fields only
Add a manual review step before any copied content is executed
Use separate workspaces for support text and data-engineering artifacts
Disable any automation that treats imported text as commands

B_data_leakage.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, interaction history, orders, and messages, and it has broad network egress. RisingWave touches no data classes in the profile and has no egress, so the main leakage risk is Chatwoot exporting sensitive support data into downstream analytics or logs. The pairwise pathway exists in default integrations, but direct evidence of a shared workspace is absent.
conditions: IF Chatwoot exports customer messages or orders into RisingWave pipelines
IF support transcripts are replicated into analytics tables or logs accessible outside the support boundary
mitigations: Mask customer identifiers before export
Limit exported columns to non-sensitive aggregates
Turn off unnecessary Chatwoot integrations
Set retention limits on downstream analytics tables
Review access controls on any shared warehouse or sink

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Chatwoot has broad network egress, while RisingWave is documented with no network egress and no write surfaces or mutable shared resources are listed for either agent. That makes direct write-write conflict unlikely from the profiles alone. Uncertainty remains because the orchestrator and storage topology are undocumented, so the safer choice is low rather than none.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mutable external resource not shown in the profiles
IF an operator adds a shared database, git repo, or filesystem mount
mitigations: Keep each agent on separate credentials
Avoid shared writable directories
Document any shared sink before enabling writes
Use read-only exports from Chatwoot into RisingWave

D_cascading_error.rationale: Chatwoot can produce customer-facing content and reports, and RisingWave is a data-engineering system that may consume those outputs downstream. There is no documented verification step between them, so if RisingWave treats Chatwoot output as authoritative, errors can cascade into analytics or operational decisions. The pathway is inferred, not directly evidenced, so medium fits.
conditions: IF RisingWave ingests Chatwoot-generated reports or messages without validation
IF downstream jobs use Chatwoot output as source-of-truth records
mitigations: Add schema validation before ingestion
Require human approval for high-impact downstream jobs
Tag Chatwoot-derived records as untrusted
Compare sampled records against source systems

E_compliance.rationale: Chatwoot handles customer data and messages, which can include regulated personal data, while RisingWave is a data-engineering platform with no documented residency or retention controls in the profile. The pair therefore creates a compliance-mismatch risk if support data is exported into analytics or streaming pipelines with different retention or jurisdiction rules. RisingWave is the only relevant cited agent for the control gap, but Chatwoot supplies the sensitive data source.
conditions: IF customer support data is streamed into RisingWave without a retention policy match
IF EU or other regulated personal data is processed in a region or system lacking the required controls
mitigations: Confirm data residency for every sink
Align retention settings across both systems
Exclude regulated fields from exports
Record a data-processing agreement for any shared pipeline
